title: Research Bite #16: Initial Practice Performance Moderates the Distributed Practice Effect in Complex Procedural Knowledge
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #16 covers Ruitenburg and colleagues' study of distributed practice in primary-school mathematical problem-solving, which asks not just whether spacing out practice sessions beats massing them together, but whether the size of that spacing advantage depends on how well a student was already performing when practice began. The study finds an inverted-U relationship: distributed practice delivers its most reliable benefit for students whose initial practice performance sits in a medium band, roughly 35%–75%. Below that band, students haven't yet grasped enough of the material for spacing alone to help — they need re-exposure through corrective feedback or restudy, with shorter, expanding gaps between practice attempts to keep retrieval within reach. Above that band, students have already essentially mastered the task, so short spacing intervals feel too easy to generate the “desirable difficulty” that makes distributed practice work — the fix there is longer, expanding intervals that make retrieval effortful again. Only in the middle band can distributed practice be adopted with confidence as a default. Barton's implication for maths teachers and textbook authors is a genuine complication of the usual “just space it out” advice on retrieval practice: how well students are already doing at the start of spaced practice should shape how that spacing is designed, not just whether it's used.
points: The inverted-U relationship — distributed practice most reliably helps students with medium (35%–75%) initial performance — directly complicates the standard blanket advice to “just space practice out,” since the study finds the benefit is not uniform across ability levels.

For students below 35% initial performance, the paper's remedy is not simply more spacing but re-exposure through corrective feedback or restudy, using shorter, expanding intervals to keep retrieval attempts within reach rather than frustratingly difficult.

For students above 75% initial performance, the recommended fix is the opposite — longer, expanding intervals — because short gaps feel too easy to preserve the “desirable difficulty” that makes distributed practice effective for material already close to mastered.

The explicit call to mathematics textbook authors, not just classroom teachers, to build initial-performance-sensitive spacing into materials is a notable practical extension beyond the usual teacher-facing implications in the series.

Because the effect is specifically demonstrated for complex procedural knowledge in primary maths problem-solving, the finding sits usefully alongside — and complicates — the more general spacing research summarized elsewhere in the archive (e.g., Research Bite #53's meta-analysis on spacing and retrieval practice in mathematics).
quotes: Ruitenburg et al.’s research investigates the impact of distributed practice on primary school students’ mathematical problem-solving abilities. The study explores whether spacing out practice sessions, as opposed to massing them together, improves long-term retention of complex procedural knowledge.
The findings suggest that distributed practice is most beneficial for students with a medium level of initial proficiency.

The study suggests an inverted U-shaped relationship between initial practice performance and the size of the spacing effect. Distributed practice is most beneficial when initial practice performance falls within approximately 35%-75%

If initial practice performance is low (less than 35%), re-exposure to the content through corrective feedback or restudy is needed. Shorter, expanding interstudy intervals should be used to make students’ retrieval and application successful.
If initial practice performance is high (more than 75%), longer, expanding interstudy intervals should be used to make students’ retrieval and application not only successful but also effortful.

Distributed practice leads to better long- term problem-solving performance than massed practice, but only for students with medium initial practice performance who have not yet completely mastered the task
